headline: High: shared filesystem, MCP, and broad shell/write privileges make prompt injection, leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can use MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent B has clipboard, workspace files, and MCP access. B’s shared local filesystem and open editor buffers create a plausible bridge for A’s outputs to be re-ingested as instructions. This is not proven by direct interaction evidence, so uncertainty stays medium rather than high.
conditions: IF A writes instruction-like content into a shared file or MCP channel that B reads automatically, injection is possible.
IF B copies A-generated text from clipboard or open buffers into its agent loop, prompt hijack risk increases.
mitigations: Disable shared clipboard transfer between the two agents.
Separate their workspaces into different directories.
Require manual review before B ingests any file produced by A.
Turn off MCP endpoints not needed for the task.
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to files and MCP messages.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches code, repository metadata, task prompts, and Ed25519 signatures, and B reads/writes workspace files with broad network egress to model providers. Because B can ingest local files and send context to third parties, sensitive material from A can leak through the shared filesystem or editor buffers in default use. The pairwise pathway is directly supported by both profiles.
conditions: IF A stores prompts, signatures, or repository metadata in a shared workspace, B can read them.
IF B forwards open files or workspace context to external model providers, those contents can leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep A and B in separate directories.
Remove secrets from any shared workspace before B runs.
Disable B network egress for sensitive projects.
Use a throwaway workspace for A’s outputs.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. B explicitly shares state with other instances via the local filesystem, while A supports multiple instances and background worker dispatch. That overlap creates a real write/write conflict on the same repo or workspace, with possible irreversible git corruption or conflicting package changes.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same repository checkout, concurrent git writes can collide.
IF both install packages or edit the same files without locking, state corruption is possible.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate clones.
Serialize git writes with a lock file.
Disable one agent’s package-install step.
Assign disjoint file paths per agent.
requires-engineering: add workspace-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A’s outputs can flow into B through files, MCP, or copied text, and B’s agent loop can act on open files and workspace context with auto-run in Yolo mode. That makes A’s unverified content a plausible authoritative input for B, which can then execute shell or git actions. The default pathway can therefore cascade from a bad suggestion into concrete downstream actions.
conditions: IF B consumes A-produced files or MCP outputs without verification, errors can propagate.
IF B is in Yolo mode, a mistaken instruction can become an executed command or commit.
mitigations: Require human approval for any action derived from A’s output.
Add a verification step before B executes commands.
Keep A’s outputs in read-only review artifacts.
Disable Yolo mode for shared tasks.
requires-engineering: implement source-tracking and confidence gating.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles task prompts, repository metadata, and signatures, while B handles open files, clipboard contents, and model-provider API calls. The profiles do not show a specific residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different retention-sensitive data classes and third-party transmission paths. Because the compliance posture is underspecified, the safer choice is medium.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace, B may transmit it to external providers.
IF retention or deletion requirements apply to A’s prompts or B’s open files, the pair may violate policy.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the shared workspace.
Review provider privacy settings before use.
Disable cloud model routing for sensitive files.
Document retention expectations for both tools.
requires-engineering: map data classes to approved processing regions.
